etymology.text: 时 ‘time’ + 候 ‘to wait; season, moment’.
etymology.src: morphemes: 时 + 候 (Wiktionary (kaikki.org) character entries)

funFacts: 时候 is the moment, 时间 the time you have: 我没有时间 ‘I have no time’ — never *没有时候.
pitfalls: …的时候 comes AFTER the clause: 我吃饭的时候 ‘when I eat’ — English when and German wenn come first.
For ‘I have no time’ use 时间, not 时候.
Not a question: …的时候 is ‘when’ in a statement; the question ‘when?’ is 什么时候 (你什么时候来？).
subtleties: In careful speech 在 opens the frame: 在我小的时候 ‘when I was little’.
In writing the short …时 replaces …的时候: 吃饭时 ‘while eating’, 到北京时 ‘when (we) arrived in Beijing’.

absent.reason: Chinese uses no preposition for a clock time: the time word itself stands before the verb.
absent.use: time + verb: 我七点吃早饭 ‘I have breakfast at seven’; 我们下午三点见 ‘let’s meet at 3 p.m.’. Formal writing may open with 在 (在下午三点), never in everyday speech.

absent.reason: Chinese uses no preposition for a day: the day word stands before the verb (or at the start).
absent.use: 星期一我工作 / 我星期一工作 ‘I work on Monday’; 五月一号放假 ‘there is a holiday on May 1st’. Formal 在 is possible (在星期一), but not with 今天 / 明天 / 昨天.

absent.reason: Chinese uses no preposition for a month, a season or a year: the time word stands before the verb.
absent.use: 我五月去北京 ‘I go to Beijing in May’; 冬天很冷 ‘it is cold in winter’; 2008年 … ‘in 2008 …’. Written style may add 在 (在2008年); to say what a month contains, 在 is the verb ‘to be in’: 我的生日在二月.
